title: Marhaba — nice to meet you
goal: Greet people the way they really do in the Levant, say your name and where you're from, and understand why Levantine Arabic has no word for "is".
bekal: greet with مَرْحَبَا and answer it the typical Levantine way
ask how someone is, with the right form for a man and for a woman
build complete sentences without a single verb

dialogs.title: حَكِي — بِالْمَقْهَى
dialogs.intro: A coffee shop in Beirut, late afternoon. Budi has been in Lebanon for two days and is sitting at the table next to a man about his age.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.literal: good, praise be to God. and you?

lines.speaker: سَامِر:
lines.literal: praise be to God. what name-your?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: My name is Budi. And you?

lines.speaker: سَامِر:
lines.id: I'm Samer. Nice to meet you.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Nice to meet you. Are you from here?

lines.speaker: سَامِر:
lines.baca: ēh, ana min Bēruut. w inta?
lines.id: Yes, I'm from Beirut. And you?
lines.literal: yes, I from Beirut. and you?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: أَنَا مِن إِنْدُونِيسْيَا. أَنَا طَالِب هُون.
lines.baca: ana min Induuniisya. ana ṭaalib hōn.
lines.id: I'm from Indonesia. I'm a student here.
lines.literal: I from Indonesia. I student here.

notes: **A greeting that doubles itself.** The most common greeting in the Levant is مَرْحَبَا *marhaba*, and the answer isn't the same word again but **the word multiplied**: مَرْحَبْتَين *marhabtēn* ("marhaba twice"). The same pattern works for أَهْلًا *ahlan*, answered with أَهْلَين *ahlēn*. Answering with the same word is still understood, but it sounds like a foreigner reciting a textbook.

**There are two forms of "you", and you can't pick at random.** To a man: كِيفَك *kēfak*. To a woman: كِيفِك *kēfik*. The difference is just one vowel, but using the wrong one is instantly noticeable. The rule applies to almost every word in this book that ends in ـَك or ـِك.

**There is no word for "is".** The sentence أَنَا طَالِب *ana ṭaalib* is literally just "I student", and that is already a complete, correct sentence. This is where Arabic is easier than English, which insists on *am*.

**The most typically Levantine "thank you" is not شُكْرًا.** What you'll hear most is يِسْلَمُوا *yislamu*, literally "may (your hands) be safe". The word شُكْرًا *shukran* is still correct and used, but it feels a little more formal.

**The little word عَم marks "-ing".** In عَم بِتْعَلَّم *‘am bit‘allam* ("I'm learning"), the word عَم has no meaning of its own — it only tells you the action is happening now. We take it apart in unit 8; for now, learn the sentence as a whole.

**Saying goodbye comes with many options, all of them polite.** Neutral: سَلَام *salaam*. Warm: بَشُوفَك *bashuufak* ("see you"). Night-time only: تِصْبَح عَ خَير *tiṣbah ‘a khēr*, answered with وْإِنْتَ مِن أَهْلُو *w inta min ahlu*.

grammars.title: Personal pronouns — and the two forms of "you"
body: Levantine Arabic has eight personal pronouns, one more than English, because "you" is split into male and female. Learn this table now: almost every unit after this one leans on it.
after: Notice the forms for "he" and "she", which end in a doubled ـِّي, as in هُوِّ and in هِيِّ. In Fusha (Modern Standard Arabic) they are هُوَ and هِيَ. Small changes like this are the quickest sign that what you're hearing is dialect, not the TV news.
The words سِتّ and رِجَّال are not used as pronouns. To speak politely to someone older, Levantine speakers still use إِنْتَ — only the tone changes.

grammars.title: Sentences without a verb
body: This is the first sentence type you need to master, and the good news is that it's simpler than English: no "am", "is" or "are". Just put the who, then the what.
after: To make it a question, you **don't need to add anything** — just raise your voice at the end. The sentence إِنْتَ طَالِب can mean "you're a student" or "you're a student?", just like casual spoken English.

To negate it, put مِش *mish* in front of the second part: أَنَا مِش طَالِب *ana mish ṭaalib* ("I'm not a student"). This مِش is the "not" for nouns and adjectives; verbs have a different "not", which we cover in unit 2.

blocks.text: Notice how صَبَاح الْخَير is answered with صَبَاح النُّور: "morning of goodness" is answered with "morning of light". Levantine speakers like to raise the stakes — you'll also hear صَبَاح الْوَرْد ("morning of roses") and صَبَاح الْيَاسْمِين ("morning of jasmine"), especially in Damascus, the city of jasmine.

blocks.title: When to use the Islamic greeting, when a neutral one
items: The greeting اَلسَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُم is used widely all over the Levant, including at work and on TV, and not only among Muslims.
In Lebanon and parts of Syria, where people follow many faiths, the neutral greeting that is always safe is مَرْحَبَا or أَهْلًا. Both are polite and carry no religious overtones.
With someone clearly older or more senior, add a respectful title after your greeting: أُسْتَاذ *ustaaz* for a man and مَدَام *madaam* for a woman.

blocks.text: In many places, "how are you?" can be skipped when you're in a hurry. In the Levant it almost can't — and it's usually asked more than once, in different words, before getting down to business. Skipping it feels cold.

The answer مَاشِي الْحَال *maashi el-haal* ("the situation is walking") is roughly "not bad" or "so-so": nothing wrong, nothing special, and it invites no follow-up questions. If things really are great, use كِلّ شِي تَمَام *kill shi tamaam* ("everything's fine").

blocks.title: Three filler words that make you sound natural
items: The word يَعْنِي *ya‘ni* works exactly like "like" or "I mean" — a filler while you build the next sentence in your head. Very handy for beginners.
The word خَلَص *khalaṣ* means "done", "enough" or "oh well", depending on the tone. It ends conversations, turns down offers and accepts how things are.
The word يَلَّا *yalla* means "come on" and also "OK, then". It moves the conversation to the next step, and people in the Levant say it dozens of times a day.

exercises.prompt: Translate into Levantine Arabic. Write the vowel marks.
items: Hi! How are you? (to a man)
Are you a student here? (to a man)

exercises.prompt: Choose the right answer to each greeting. Write it out in full.
items: Your friend says مَرْحَبَا. You answer ____.
Your friend says أَهْلًا. You answer ____.
You walk into a shop at eight in the morning and greet with ____.
The shopkeeper answers your morning greeting with ____.
Before bed your friend says تِصْبَح عَ خَير. You answer ____.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: مَرْحَبَا! كِيفَك؟ — مْنِيح، اَلْحَمْدُ لِلَّه. — شُو اِسْمِك؟ — اِسْمِي بُودِي. — أَنَا مِن إِنْدُونِيسْيَا. — إِنْتَ طَالِب هُون؟
أَنَا — إِنْتَ — هِيِّ — نِحْنَا — إِنْتُو — هُوِّ
مَرْحَبْتَين. — أَهْلَين. — صَبَاح الْخَير. — صَبَاح النُّور. — وْإِنْتَ مِن أَهْلُو.
أَنَا طَالِب هُون. — شُو اِسْمَك؟ — هُوِّ مِن بَيْرُوت. — إِنْتِي مْنِيحَة؟ — نِحْنَا مِن إِنْدُونِيسْيَا. — أَنَا مِش مُدَرِّس.
wave: Today, greet five people in your head — three men and two women — and make sure you use كِيفَك and كِيفِك in the right places.
